:::{#exm-quadratic-big-o}
#### A quadratic is $O(n^2)$ but not $O(n)$

Let $f(n) = 3n^2 + 5n$.

For $n \ge 5$, we have $5n \le n \cdot n = n^2$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(n)
&= 3n^2 + 5n \\
&\le 3n^2 + n^2 \\
&= 4n^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

So $f(n) = O(n^2)$, with $c = 4$ and $n_0 = 5$ in @def-big-o.
Since $f(n) \ge 3n^2$ for every $n$, also $f(n) = \Omega(n^2)$,
and so $f(n) = \Theta(n^2)$.

But $f(n)$ is not $O(n)$.
If it were, there would be $c > 0$ and $n_0$ with $3n^2 + 5n \le c \, n$
for every $n \ge n_0$.
Dividing both sides by $n > 0$ gives $3n + 5 \le c$ for every $n \ge n_0$,
which fails once $n > (c - 5)/3$.

:::
